newsitem.title: GERMANY: German opposition leader throws weight behind EMU.
newsitem.headline: German opposition leader throws weight behind EMU.

text.p: The chairman of Germany's opposition Social Democrats (SPD) delivered a rousing defence of Europe's planned single currency on Tuesday only days after his main party rival called for the project to be postponed.
Oskar Lafontaine told a party conference in Berlin that the Euro currency, due to be introduced in 1999, was a tool to fight unemployment in the European Union.
His firm stand contrasted with a call by Lower Saxony state premier Gerhard Schroeder on Saturday for a delay in the planned economic and monetary union (EMU).
Lafontaine and Schroeder are the two leading candidates to become the SPD's challenger to Chancellor Helmut Kohl in the 1998 general elections.
Lafontaine also called for harmonisation of European tax policies to prohibit individual countries from using low taxation rates for their economic advantage.
Schroeder came in for heavy criticism, even within the SPD, for saying Germany would not meet the Maastricht criteria for a single currency on time and should therefore delay its launch.

Germany's six top economic institutes said in their autumn forecast on Tuesday that the 1997 deficit would be 3.5 percent of gross domestic product -- above the Maastricht treaty's three percent goal for joining monetary union planned in 1999.
But Finance Minister Theo Waigel, an advocate of a strict reading of Maastricht, said "the conditions will be created" in final budget talks to bring the deficit below three percent.

The SPD has been anxious to distance itself from an anti-Euro platform after suffering spectacular losses in March this year with a regional election campaign that even many Social Democrats linked to right-wing "D-mark nationalism."
